content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Shepherd/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

You are mining ONE captured agent-conversation log from the Shepherd repo (missingbulb/Shepherd) for durable, reusable lessons, per the "extract-from-conversations" method. This is a research task — do not edit any files, just report findings.

## How to get the log
Run: `git show "origin/conversation-logs:2026-08-17T2002Z--issue-28--be45aff4-0993-5089-8959-570a08bb6d85.jsonl" > /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Shepherd/f1bb38f5-c28e-580d-a7dd-074a6cfe5b3c/scratchpad/log-issue-28.jsonl` (use exactly this unique output filename — do not reuse a generic name since other agents are doing this concurrently on other files). Then read/grep that file. It's a JSONL of one Claude Code session's turns, tool calls, and timestamps.

## What counts as a lesson (the bar)
A signal is only worth reporting if the fix is durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one session — NOT a one-off situational detail, NOT a restatement of a generic truism, NOT something already implied by an existing rule. Read end-to-end and hunt for:
1. **Misunderstandings** — a clarifying round-trip, the user correcting an assumption, the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it, an AskUserQuestion whose answer was an obvious default.
2. **Suboptimal agent actions** — backtracking, redundant/repeated work, re-running an already-failed command, using a heavy tool where a light one fit, reinventing something the codebase already provided, missing an existing convention.
3. **Long wall-time waits** — MEASURE with real timestamps from the log. Independent ops run serially that could've been parallel, a padded/blind sleep, polling after the result was already available, re-checking an already-green CI check. Quantify actual wall-clock seconds/minutes lost, don't hand-wave.

This log's issue (#28) is referenced in the existing RULES.md as one of the sessions burning 17-105 minutes of human-round-trip idle time on AskUserQuestion calls whose answer was already decided or the default. Look for OTHER lessons beyond that already-documented one.

Do NOT report: an already-settled/enforced implementation choice; the owner's personal preferences (tone, merge-word, summary style); the agent framework's own loading mechanics (why a skill didn't mount, etc — that's a bug to file upstream, not a project rule); a gotcha tied to one call site (that belongs as a code comment, not a pack rule, so drop it, don't report it here).

## Dedup against what's ALREADY in this repo's local pack
Read the actual file at /home/user/Shepherd/.claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/RULES.md before starting (it's checked out locally in this container) — do NOT report anything that duplicates, restates, or is already implied by an existing bullet there (even if worded differently). Only report something genuinely NEW.

## What to report back
For each genuinely new candidate lesson (there may be zero — that's a fine and common outcome, most sessions yield nothing):

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Shepherd/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

Shepherd's own fleet-usage task recomputes this file daily, so it was left out
of the digest migration on the reasoning that nothing is lost. That was only
half right: the recompute is stateless, but its inputs are each member's own

This was deliberately left out of #23 on the reasoning that Shepherd's own `fleet-usage` task recomputes the file daily, so nothing is lost. That was only half right. The recompute *is* stateless, but its inputs are each member's own `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json` over the window that member still keeps — so a fresh run would start the series from a shorter history than the one Sheepdog had accumulated, and the earlier weeks would simply not come back.

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

input.prompt:
You are mining ONE captured agent-conversation log from the Shepherd repo (missingbulb/Shepherd) for durable, reusable lessons, per the "extract-from-conversations" method. This is a research task — do not edit any files, just report findings.

## How to get the log
Run: `git show "origin/conversation-logs:2026-08-28T1638Z--issue-306--8b504739-749a-5fb9-a026-186390285e5e.jsonl" > /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Shepherd/f1bb38f5-c28e-580d-a7dd-074a6cfe5b3c/scratchpad/log-issue-306.jsonl` (use exactly this unique output filename — do not reuse a generic name since other agents are doing this concurrently on other files). Then read/grep that file. It's a JSONL of one Claude Code session's turns, tool calls, and timestamps.

This session's issue (#306) was a "claudinite-dashboard/fleet-digest" task: reading a shortlist of ranked candidate PRs/issues from a data branch and picking the strongest ones to write a dated digest brief. It resulted in PR #311 (a single-file digest addition, merged with no review comments).

## What counts as a lesson (the bar)
A signal is only worth reporting if the fix is durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one session — NOT a one-off situational detail, NOT a restatement of a generic truism, NOT something already implied by an existing rule. Read end-to-end and hunt for:
1. **Misunderstandings** — a clarifying round-trip, the user correcting an assumption, the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it, an AskUserQuestion whose answer was an obvious default.
2. **Suboptimal agent actions** — backtracking, redundant/repeated work, re-running an already-failed command, using a heavy tool where a light one fit, reinventing something the codebase already provided, missing an existing convention.
3. **Long wall-time waits** — MEASURE with real timestamps from the log. Independent ops run serially that could've been parallel, a padded/blind sleep, polling after the result was already available, re-checking an already-green CI check. Quantify actual wall-clock seconds/minutes lost, don't hand-wave.

Do NOT report: an already-settled/enforced implementation choice; the owner's personal preferences (tone, merge-word, summary style); the agent framework's own loading mechanics (why a skill didn't mount, etc — that's a bug to file upstream, not a project rule); a gotcha tied to one call site (that belongs as a code comment, not a pack rule, so drop it, don't report it here).

## Dedup against what's ALREADY in this repo's local pack
Read the actual file at /home/user/Shepherd/.claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/RULES.md before starting (it's checked out locally in this container) — do NOT report anything that duplicates, restates, or is already implied by an existing bullet there (even if worded differently). Only report something genuinely NEW.

## What to report back
For each genuinely new candidate lesson (there may be zero — that's a fine and common outcome, most sessions yield nothing, especially for a short mechanical curation task like this one):
- One terse imperative rule sentence (repo-specific voice, matching the existing RULES.md style — pattern is usually "**Doing X** — do Y, because Z (#<issue>)")

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Shepherd/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request

How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.

## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest

Your task's declared `expected_outcome` is a **ceiling, not a plan**:

- **`open-pr`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
  applies to you.
- **`merged-pr`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.

## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference

`.claudinite-settings.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:

- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading `merged-pr`
  to open-pr is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
  materializing it is the update converge's job, not yours.
- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the work item.

## 2. Arm auto-merge

Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
it once this repo's required checks pass.

## 3. When the arm is rejected

- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
  PR's **head sha**:
  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the `merged-pr` ceiling — the trail
    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
    unseen check does not survive anything.

## Never

Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
are always legal outcomes.

Answers, one per question:

**1. The workflows — they were wired.** `converge-wiring.mjs` produced both `claudinite-scheduler.yml` (hourly tick, cron minute `11`) and `claudinite-executor.yml` (the label-triggered pull worker), and both were in the first commit. If they're not showing up for you, it may be that Actions doesn't run workflows from a PR branch until they exist on `main`.

**2. The CCR routine — you're right, and my reasoning was backwards.** I read the executor *workflow* as having replaced the routine, and told you an endpoint would be "dead config." What `invoke.mjs` actually does is resolve `taskScheduler.endpoints.default` for any task that declares no `invocation_endpoint` — absence means *use the default key*, not *needs nothing*. Eleven of the eighteen declared tasks are agentic; every one of them would have hit `no invocation endpoint "default"` and parked on `needs-human`. The two-workflow shape misled me: the executor workflow is the pull worker, and it *fires* the routine.

Fixed in `7fc520b`: routine `Claudinite executor - Shepherd` (`trig_01Xc43XQwqjUgTaFQhXvAJdk`) created, endpoint configured, re-converged so `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` is stamped into the executor's env. One correction to bootstrap's Part 6 step 5 while I was there — its prompt points at `executor.md`, which is the *slots*-mode instruction file; this repo defaults to queue mode, so the routine points at `queue/instructions.md`.

**3. The setup issue — no excuse.** The basics pack is explicit: a human-only step gets *its own issue*, with a checkbox each, what breaks while it's off, and a closing condition — "never a note in the PR body." I put it in the PR body. That's now **#3**, covering both secrets, auto-merge/squash/Actions settings, the routine's UI fields, the environment script, and retiring `sheepdog` from the Sheepdog repo. One thing I'd missed entirely: the API can't pass connectors through, so the routine as created has no GitHub MCP tools — and the executor's instructions say its GitHub access is MCP-only. That's a checkbox now.

I also skipped the task issue itself, which the lifecycle requires *before* starting — that's **#2**, filed late.

**4. No, bootstrapping still asks for all of it.** Nothing was dropped upstream; I under-delivered. The one place bootstrap.md genuinely lags the engine is that Part 6 step 5 prompt.

**One genuinely new lesson clears the bar:**

- **Declaring Shepherd as a role a predecessor repo already filled** (pointing the `claude-code-web-users-support` preferences store at `missingbulb/Shepherd` during the Sheepdog→Shepherd handoff) — copy the predecessor's actual content into the new repo in the *same* change that declares the role, and check the very next session-start hook output as the verification, rather than trusting the config wiring alone. The hook printed `USER PREFERENCES: ... could not be read (no preferences file for this user)` twice in this session's own tool output (12:20:34 and again at 12:27:54) before the owner had to point out the missing `Sheepdog/preferences` directory at 12:43:31 — over 20 minutes where the failure was sitting in the agent's own transcript, unactioned, until a human caught it (#2).

(#2, #22, #28, #32)". Reporting it again would be a pure duplicate.
- A missed `Comment class:` line caught by the Stop hook, and a `tail`-truncated exit code that caused a command to be re-run — both are instances of already-existing general rules being imperfectly followed, not new coverage gaps.

**One genuinely new candidate:**

**Waiting on a PR's CI check** — poll `pull_request_read get_check_runs` directly on a short interval and act the moment it returns; don't *also* launch a background `sleep`/`until` wait job as a hedge alongside the direct poll. Twice in this same session a background wait command was spawned for exactly this purpose and was moot before it even had a chance to matter: at 20:31:58Z a 40s background wait was launched for CI to finish on PR #34, but the check had already completed 3 seconds *earlier* (20:31:55Z) per the direct poll — the background job's only effect was a spurious task-notification 40s later that cost an extra turn to dismiss ("nothing new to act on"). It recurred at 08:45:57Z (a 45s wait after pushing the merge-conflict resolution): the direct polls at 08:46:01Z/08:46:04Z already showed the check `completed`/`success`, and the PR was merged by 08:46:13Z — 32 seconds before the background wait would even finish. (#32)

I'm reporting only this one — it's measurable, recurred twice in one session, and isn't implied by the existing "don't manufacture a no-op Bash call between notifications" rule (that one covers idling once a background task is *already* dispatched; this covers not dispatching the redundant background wait in the first place when direct polling is faster and already sufficient).

All 7 agents have reported. Two lessons survive dedup:

1. **Issue #2** — declaring this repo as a store for a role a retiring predecessor filled (the preferences-store declaration during the Sheepdog→Shepherd handoff) without copying content, then missing the session's own hook diagnostic reporting the gap for 20+ minutes.
2. **Issue #32** — launching a redundant background CI-wait job as a hedge alongside already-sufficient direct polling, which recurred twice and only produced a spurious dismiss-turn.

Both are genuinely new, generalizable, and not already covered by existing rules; the activity half and 5 of 7 conversation logs (#22, #24, #28, #30, #306) yielded nothing. Let me pull the current RULES.md and VERSIONS.md to land these two entries correctly.

content.content:
1	# shepherd — this repo's own rules
2	
3	The capture surface for lessons **specific to this repository**. Loaded into every session
4	through the rules index, so what lands here should be a directive an agent can act on, not a
5	description of how something works.
6	
7	A lesson that would hold in another repo does not belong here — propose it to the Claudinite
8	canon instead, where every repo gets it.
9	
10	- **Reading this fleet's activity to rank or report it** — filter Claudinite's own artifacts out
11	  of **every** stream you collect, not just the first one you thought of. The machine is the
12	  busiest actor in this fleet, and its bookkeeping does not merely appear in a size-or-discussion
13	  ranking, it wins it: a dispatch issue collects a comment per executor stage, so it outweighs the
14	  work it dispatched, and a guard written for pull requests while issues go through unfiltered
15	  leaves the whole hole open. Recognize a machine artifact with the engine's own `isDispatchTitle`
16	  rather than a private regex, since the dispatch-title format is the scheduler's to change. Count
17	  the maintenance total where it is **tallied**, never by dropping items in the fetch: an issue the
18	  machinery filed and closed is still a true account of how much of the day this fleet spent
19	  servicing itself.
20	
21	- **Carrying an artifact directory over from a repo being retired** (the Sheepdog → Shepherd
22	  fleet-enforcer handoff) — verify the *machinery that produces it* came over too, not just its
23	  historical output. `digests/`'s files landed in #23 and read as fully carried; the missing
24	  generator (Sheepdog's `sheepdog-local` pack and its `fleet-digest` task) surfaced only later, in
25	  #27, once checked separately from the output. A copied output folder visually launders the
26	  absence of its live producer — audit for the generator explicitly, in the same pass, rather than
27	  inferring it from the presence of past output.
28	
29	- **Dropping a folded/aggregate `GENERATED` file because "the next run recomputes it"** — check
30	  first whether the recompute's own *inputs* retain the same history the current output does. A
31	  stateless recompute over inputs each fleet member keeps only for a bounded window starts the
32	  series shorter than a file carried over from elsewhere already holds — nearly true of
33	  `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json`, first left out of the Sheepdog carryover (#23) on exactly that
34	  assumption, then copied over verbatim once the gap was caught (#31). "The generator will refill
35	  it" is not sufficient on its own; confirm the generator's inputs cover the same span first.
36	
37	- **Scoping a fleet-wide text/reference sweep from this repo** — don't trust
38	  `mcp__github__search_code` alone to enumerate the affected member repos; its index can lag and
39	  silently undercount. Cross-check against the full known member roster (fetch each member's
40	  `.claudinite-checks.json` directly) before scoping the sweep: a Sheepdog-reference sweep found
41	  only 3 repos via search but 11 by direct check (#24).
42	
43	- **Renaming, adding, or removing a pack in `.claudinite-checks.json`** — re-run
44	  `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs missingbulb/Shepherd --badges` in
45	  the same change. The README's `<!-- claudinite:packs -->` badge row is a one-time seed the
46	  update flow deliberately never re-derives, so it silently goes stale on every declaration
47	  change and only resurfaces later as a blocking `reference-integrity` finding — this exact gap
48	  hit twice, once for the `core`/`grow_with_claudinite` rename (#67, fixed in #69) and again for
49	  the `sheepdog` → `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` rename (#79, fixed in #80/#81).
50	
51	- **Waiting on this repo's PR CI** — it's a single `checks` job that completes in roughly 7–15
52	  seconds (measured directly across #30, #32, #59, #67). Poll `pull_request_read get_check_runs`
53	  in a short loop instead of a fixed or backgrounded `sleep`, and don't call
54	  `enable_pr_auto_merge` in the same breath as opening the PR — GitHub refuses it with "unstable
55	  status" if the check hasn't started yet, which is a sign to wait and re-poll, not license to
56	  merge by hand instead (#59). Before stating a PR's status in a closing callout, read
57	  `get_check_runs` rather than asserting "CI running" as an unread guess (#30), and skip grepping
58	  `.github/workflows/*.yml` to guess whether a workflow gates the merge — the check runs already
59	  say so directly (#60).
60	
61	- **Firing an `AskUserQuestion`** — check first whether the answer is already decided: by a rule
62	  already loaded in context, by fleet or repo state one read away (a sibling's
63	  `.claudinite-checks.json`, a pending adoption interview), or by the option marked
64	  "(Recommended)" simply being the status quo. Batch every open decision a run will need into one
65	  question instead of asking serially. Four sessions lost 17 to 105 minutes of pure
66	  human-round-trip idle time to questions whose answer was already available or was the presented
67	  default (#2, #22, #28, #32).
68	
69	- **Leaving multiple PRs open for the owner after a fleet-wide sweep** — call
70	  `subscribe_pr_activity` on every one of them, not a sample. #24's sweep subscribed only 2 of 12
71	  open PRs, then spent over two hours and ~29 API calls re-polling the other 10 on a self-armed
72	  hourly wake-up with zero state change, while the 2 subscribed PRs' merges arrived instantly as
73	  activity events the moment the owner acted.
74	
75	- **Triaging a `fleet-drift` issue that names another repo** — don't spend a call on
76	  `mcp__github__get_file_contents` (or any other repo-scoped MCP read) against that repo: this
77	  session's GitHub access is scoped to `missingbulb/Shepherd` only, and every cross-repo call is
78	  denied outright. Five separate triage subagents each independently spent a call rediscovering
79	  that denial before falling back to the only place the answer actually lives — the issue body's
80	  own self-description of how the item converges (#104).
81	
82	- **Hunting for this repo's own standing tracker issue by its exact title** —
83	  `mcp__github__search_issues` with a quoted title and `in:title` does not reliably filter; it can
84	  return the same broad, unfiltered issue list regardless of the query text, burying the real
85	  tracker in a couple dozen unrelated hits (and once, overflowing the token cap entirely). The same

  work it dispatched, and a guard written for pull requests while issues go through unfiltered
  leaves the whole hole open. Recognize a machine artifact with the engine's own `isDispatchTitle`
  rather than a private regex, since the dispatch-title format is the scheduler's to change. Count
  the maintenance total where it is **tallied**, never by dropping items in the fetch: an issue the
  machinery filed and closed is still a true account of how much of the day this fleet spent
  servicing itself.

  absence of its live producer — audit for the generator explicitly, in the same pass, rather than

  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the work item.

## 2. Arm auto-merge

Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
it once this repo's required checks pass.

## 3. When the arm is rejected

- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.

  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
  PR's **head sha**:

    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the `merged-pr` ceiling — the trail
    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
    unseen check does not survive anything.

## Never

Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
are always legal outcomes.
